ledger.issue: The restore's check batches are pinned as functions and cannot be driven or checkpointed from the Spec. This is beside r3-architecture-restore-and-baseline-migration-disagree, which is about what the checks accept. (1) No runner. `streamCheckBatch`, `readModelCheckBatch`, `receiptCheckBatch` and `pendingWorkBatch` each return 'whether the enumeration is done', the reviewed bullet says 'no check batch ... schedules anything', and the workflow only says 'The journal check runs in batches'. Nothing says what calls a batch again: an operator by hand, a script, or a chain. do-nothing-check says the opposite, 'the plain scheduled mutations that remain are the platform's own maintenance batches, rebuild, baseline migration and restore checks'. The L2-8 example asserts 'all four checks reach `passed`' without saying what ran them. (2) The checkpoint does not fit the work. `restoreRuns.checks` 'holds five entries', each with one `cursor: v.optional(v.string())`, but `streamCheckBatch` takes `{ runId, contextId, streamType, scope }` and `readModelCheckBatch` takes `{ runId, readModel, scope }`: with two contexts, several read models and, under `all`, every tenant, one string cannot say which source, tenant and page a check has reached, and nothing says when a check's `state` becomes `passed`. (3) The stream check resumes inside a page: on `budgetExhausted` 'the batch saves the cursor at that stream and returns', but the `paginator` cursor the context returns marks the end of a page, and no call gives a cursor at a stream inside it. (4) `readModelCheckBatch` is 'reusing the rebuild's verify logic in compare mode'. rebuild defines no compare mode: `verifyBatch` takes `{ generationId, fence }` and repairs what it finds, and for a `HistoryProjection` view 'fields equal the projection of the current DTO' has no meaning. (5) The first flow needs 'the recovery-plan entry recorded with it: commit, schema hash, configuration hash', and the operator 'confirms that the deployed schema matches the backup's schema hash'; no Spec says where that entry is kept or how either hash is computed. `getRestoreRun` is listed in `convexSurface` without a signature.
ledger.fix: In `spec:application.restore`: name the runner, either an operator-run loop that calls each batch until it returns done, stated as the procedure and used by the L2-8 example, or a self-scheduling chain that is exempt from the door, and correct the reviewed bullet or the do-nothing-check sentence to match. Replace the per-check string with a structured cursor, the registry's `BatchCursor` plus a source index, and let each batch take only `runId` and work out its next source, read model and tenant from the read-model registry that r3-architecture-one-projection-writes-every-generation asks for; say that a check is `passed` when the last tenant of the last source reports done with no finding. For the fold budget take streams one at a time with `numItems` 1, as the history batch does, or store the page cursor and an offset. Pin the shared verify helper with a `mode` of repair or compare in `spec:application.rebuild`, and rule on history views: compare by a second fold under the door, or record them as not checked. Say how the schema and configuration hashes are computed and where the recovery-plan entry lives, and give `getRestoreRun` its signature.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, APPL-10: At HEAD, restore.sdp.md:98 saves "the cursor at that stream" although the list returns only a page cursor, and :102 does not require every check to be passed, so an interrupted multi-source run has no complete runner or safe finish guard. The issue and structured enumeration or shared compare-helper fix remain right; completion must require every required check passed. The build must show: convex-test must run a complete multi-context restore, exhaust a fold budget inside a page and interrupt between checks without manual cursor reconstruction; finishing while a required check is pending must refuse. A native backend drill must complete through the declared runner.

ledger.issue: The audit path fails closed, and neither of its two writers can build the row the table requires. `fnWriteAudit` is `writeAudit(ctx: MutationCtx, record: AuditRecordInput)` and `AuditRecordInput` is defined nowhere. `tableAuditRecords` requires `operationId`, `commandType`, `subject: v.object({ contextId, streamType, streamId })`, `kind` and `decision: v.string()`. The pipeline's step 10 calls it 'for a declaration that sets `audit`', and the declaration gives only `audit?: { kind: "security" | "business" }`: `subject` has no source when the optional `permission.subjectFrom` is absent or when a use case touches many streams, as `PlaceOrder` with 101 does, `decision` has no stated values, and `causedBy` is `v.optional(v.string())` while the operation's cause is the `CausedBy` union. The second writer is the gate: write-pause says 'every close, resume and abort writes an audit record inside the same mutation and fails closed', and `closeScope` and `resumeScope` have a scope key, a reason and an actor, with no operation ID, no command type and no stream subject. baseline-operations says of the write that 'any failure, including a validator refusal or a document too large, throws and rolls the whole command back', so a wrong guess here refuses every audited command, and a gate close that cannot write its record refuses every paused rebuild.
ledger.fix: In `spec:operations.baseline-operations` define `AuditRecordInput` and give each field its source under E-43: `subject` is `decl.permission.subjectFrom(input)` when declared and otherwise the first affected ref, `decision` is the outcome kind, `causedBy` is the operation's cause in a stated string form, `requestKey` and `actor` come from the `PipelineCall`. Make the table fit an operator action: either `operationId`, `commandType` and `subject` become optional with a third `kind` of `operator` that carries `action` and `scopeKey`, or gate changes go to their own small table; say which in write-pause `fnCloseScope` and `fnResumeScope`. Repeat the field sources in the pipeline's `auditWrite` bullet so step 10 can be written from it.

ledger.issue: No Spec says how a read model gets its first active generation, and without one the command path writes nothing. The pipeline's step 9 writes 'the generations `generationsToWrite` returns', which is `{ active?: number; building?: number }` read from the `generations` table; on a fresh deployment that table is empty, so the answer is empty and no row is written, and the registry adds 'a read model with no active generation reads as empty'. The only way into `active` is the listed chain 'building to verifying, verifying to verified, verified to active', that is `startGeneration`, the backfill and verify batches and `switchGeneration`, each an operator call that also needs the tenant list of r3-architecture-tenant-list-undefined. Every rebuild example starts from 'a read model with an active generation', the L2-2 example runs `PlaceOrder` on its own disposable backend and asserts 'the next subscription value's page carries the order's summary row', and `limitExpectedDocuments` counts 'the summary row' in every measured `PlaceOrder`. None of them says who created generation 1. An implementer has to choose between running a full rebuild of an empty read model as a deploy step, which no release rule mentions, and inventing a bootstrap write that the transition list forbids.
ledger.fix: Rule it in `spec:application.generation-registry` under E-8: either the deploy that first declares a read model inserts generation 1 directly as `active` with the declared projection version, through a named internal mutation that refuses when any generation row of that read model exists, and the transition list gains 'none to active for the first generation'; or `generationsToWrite` treats a read model with no row as generation 1 active and writes the row on first use, with the cost of that write stated. Add the step to `releaseRule` in `spec:operations.baseline-operations` and to the build flows of `spec:application.first-experiment`, and have the L2-2 example say how its backend got the active generation.

ledger.issue: STATE lead 7, confirmed. `DiagnosticRecord.outcome` is '"applied" | "businessFailure" | "rejection" | "technicalFailure" | "transientRefusal"' with `errorCode?: string`, and the only emitter is the pipeline's 'Step 11, return: the mutation emits one diagnostic record', which runs after every business write on the success path. The outermost catch 'only rethrows', so a rejected, refused or failed command emits nothing, three of the five outcome values and `errorCode` are never produced, and D19's diagnosis 'by request key or operation ID' has no line for the commands that most need one. A replayed duplicate returns at step 5 and is not said to emit either. Three fields of the same record have no stated source: `durationMs`, although event-envelope says '`Date.now()` in the mutation, which Convex freezes for the whole function' and only the sweeper names `performance.now()`; `layer: number`; and `causedBy?: string` against the `CausedBy` union. `emitDiagnostic` is said to count swallowed errors by 'increments a counter in memory', which nothing can read back, while the ALL-1 example asserts 'the fixture's swallowed-error counter is one'.
ledger.fix: In `spec:operations.baseline-operations` either narrow `outcome` to the two committed kinds and drop `errorCode`, or say that the pipeline's outermost catch calls `emitDiagnostic` inside its own try before it rethrows, for rejections, transient refusals and other throws, and that a replay emits a record with `replayed` true; state which in the pipeline's `diagnosticEmit` bullet. Name `performance.now()` as the source of `durationMs`, define `layer`, give `causedBy` a string form, and replace the in-memory counter with something a test can observe, such as a second log line.

ledger.issue: Three Layer 1 and 2 jobs are pinned as functions with nothing that starts or repeats them; the first cron in the corpus is Layer 3's. (1) The receipt sweep, STATE lead 7: `receipts.sweep` is 'one `internalMutation` ... per deployment, scheduled by operations', takes `{ tenantId, now, limit }` and returns `more`; no Spec says what schedules it, what loops while `more` is true, why `now` is an argument, or where the tenants come from, which joins r3-architecture-tenant-list-undefined. Without it expired receipts that are never looked up stay for ever. (2) The purge: 'After `retireAfter`, `purgeGenerationBatch` deletes the retired generation's rows and markers in bounded batches', and aborted rows 'are purged in bounded batches'; nothing schedules the first batch or the next, `resumeChain` is 'refused with a plain error in any other state' than building or verifying, and the batch deletes 'by the `by_key` index range for that generation' although `by_key` is `["tenantId", "generation", "key"]` and the marker index also leads with the tenant, so the batch needs a tenant and a cursor its `{ generationId, fence }` arguments do not carry. The L2-6 abort example drives it by hand. (3) The import command of E-41 is one table: `imports` has `expected`, `done`, `failed`, `state`, `lastBatch` and `operationId`, the rule speaks of 'a sequence of bounded batch commands the caller drives' and 'the caller's progress query', and no function creates the row, records a batch, completes or cancels it, or reads progress, while the restore inventories its `running` rows. The `personalData` table of E-43 is in the same state: two indexes, a deletion rule, and no function that writes, reads or deletes a row.
ledger.fix: For the receipt sweep and the purge, add a `crons.interval` bullet in the Spec that owns each, as the sweeper does, or name the operator entry that runs them, and state the loop: the sweep reschedules itself while `more`, per tenant from the tenant table. Give `purgeGenerationBatch` a cursor on the generation row, tenant iteration like `tenantIteration`, and a start: `switchGeneration` or a daily cron schedules it once `retireAfter` has passed. For the import, pin `startImport`, `recordImportBatch`, `finishImport`, `cancelImport` and `getImport` with their arguments in `spec:application.parent-use-cases`, or mark the import command as written by the build that first needs it and say so under E-41. Do the same for `personalData` in `spec:operations.baseline-operations`.

ledger.issue: Small things in Layers 0 to 2 that are named and not pinned, each a short guess for the implementer. (1) `Bounds = { maxItems?: number; maxBytes?: number }` is checked 'when the input's items exceed `bounds.maxItems`', and nothing says which part of an input is its items; the L2-3 maximum example needs it to mean `lines`. (2) The pipeline lists parse as step 1 and authenticate as step 2, and parent-use-cases says the bound is 'checked by the pipeline's step 1 before authentication', but `runPipeline` takes a `PipelineCall` whose `actor` is required and the public helper 'establishes the actor ... and calls `runPipeline`', so for the public entry authentication runs first. (3) outcome-boundary says 'a code outside both is a technical failure by definition', while `normalizeThrown(error, commandType)` rethrows any bare kernel `Rejection` as a rejection and never sees the declaration's `rejections`; `irreversible` likewise 'requires' a tombstone with no check named. (4) receipt-table says 'a declaration may set a finite horizon' for `tombstoneHorizon`, and `Retention = { window; afterExpiry }` has no field for it. (5) `limitRequestKey` says a longer key 'is rejection `invalidInput` at step 1'; Step 1 and `errorCodeInvalidInput` do not mention it. (6) `canonicalJson` is defined for JSON values only; a Convex input may hold `v.int64()` or `v.bytes()`. (7) `get` returns `null` for a deleted subject 'unless the DTO policy shows deleted subjects', and no field declares that policy; `list` takes `includeDeleted` and its handler text never uses it. (8) `Journal` is the return type of `createJournal` with no members; `streamParts.streamVersion` has no rule for what is written to it or who reads it. (9) `carryOrReject(outcome, policy)` throws 'through the outcome boundary's `reject`', which requires `commandType`, and takes its `message` from nowhere. (10) `applyHistoryProjection` takes `mode: ApplyMode` and no step reads it; the `events` it is fed include `baseline` events, and the contract does not say `keyOf` must return `null` for them. (11) Validators and types used once and never given: `generationDoc`, `gateDoc`, `AuditRecordInput`, `DiagnosticSink`, `consoleSink`, and in Layer 3 `callInputValidator`, `obligationViewValidator`, `dispatchResultValidator`. (12) One bound has two names, `limitGrantsRead` in actor-and-scope and `limitGrantsPerPrincipal` in tenancy-and-authority, and the handler registry has two shapes, `HandlerRegistry` mapping to a `FunctionReference` in obligation-module while `createStep3` reads `entry.maxAttempts` from the wrapper's `HandlerEntry`. (13) `convexTypeImport` says a value import of `convex/values` 'is a type error'; `verbatimModuleSyntax` rejects only a type imported without `import type`, so `import { v }` compiles and only the dependency check catches it. (14) `limitExpectedDocuments` lists the reads of one `PlaceOrder` and leaves out the grants read of step 4. (15) The experiment's examples rely on 'the production `auth.config.ts`' and no Spec names its provider or issuer.
ledger.fix: One line each in the owning Spec: add `itemsOf?: (input: I) => number` to `Bounds` in `spec:command.command-declaration`, or say `maxItems` counts the elements of the input's one top-level array; state in the pipeline that the public entry authenticates before step 1's bound and refinement checks, and correct the parent-use-cases sentence; pass `decl.rejections` to `normalizeThrown` and rethrow an unlisted code as a plain error, or drop the 'technical failure by definition' sentence, and name the registration check as the place `irreversible` is checked; add `tombstoneHorizon?: number` to `Retention`; add the key-length check to Step 1; define `canonicalJson` over `convexToJson(value)`; add `showDeleted?: boolean` to `StreamRegistration` or drop the clause, and say `list` filters deleted rows after the page is read unless `includeDeleted`; give `Journal` its two fields and `streamParts.streamVersion` its rule or remove the field; let `carryOrReject` throw the bare kernel `Rejection` and let `normalizeThrown` add the command type; say `mode` is ignored by `applyHistoryProjection` and that `keyOf` returns `null` for `baseline`; define the listed validators beside their one use; keep one name for the grants bound and one registry type; reword `convexTypeImport`; add the grants read to `limitExpectedDocuments`; name the experiment's auth provider in `spec:application.first-experiment`.

ledger.issue: rebuild says of a backfill batch, which is a scheduled internal mutation: 'a batch that keeps losing the optimistic-concurrency race fails after Convex's own retries with its documents-changed error, and a developer error, that failure or a timeout ends the batch', and `occRace` repeats 'a batch that keeps losing fails after Convex's internal retries with its documents-changed error, which is the stall that `resumeGeneration` answers'. For a scheduled mutation the scheduling page says: 'Once scheduled, mutations are guaranteed to be executed exactly once. Convex will automatically retry any internal Convex errors, and only fail on developer errors' (docs.convex.dev/scheduling/scheduled-functions, read 2026-10-01), and the open-source scheduler shows what that means for a conflict: in `handle_mutation` an OCC error on commit runs `backoff.fail(); wait; continue` with no retry cap (get-convex/convex-backend, crates/application/src/scheduled_jobs/mod.rs, `SCHEDULER_OCC_MAX_BACKOFF` 60 seconds, read 2026-10-01). So a contended batch is never marked failed and never ends its chain. It stays pending and is retried with growing backoff, the generation row's `lastError` stays empty, and the stall shows only as an `updatedAt` that stops moving. The operator signal the Spec describes does not occur. The mechanism survives: `resumeGeneration` bumps the fence and the old batch, when it finally commits, returns on the stale fence.

State that as the stall signal in the E-40 question and in `resumeGeneration`, and keep the documents-changed error for mutations a caller invokes, as persistence-adapter `versionConflictVersusOccRetry` already has it. Mark the unbounded retry as read from the backend source, not from a docs page, and add it to Probe 6.

The built-in `.paginate()` returns five keys, not three. convex-js `src/server/impl/query_impl.ts` returns `{ page, isDone, continueCursor, splitCursor, pageStatus }`, and the backend's `queryPage` syscall serializes `split_cursor: Option<String>` and `page_status: Option<&str>` with no skip, so both keys are present as `null` on an ordinary page (get-convex/convex-js and get-convex/convex-backend crates/isolate/src/environment/udf/async_syscall.rs, read 2026-10-01). That is why `paginationResultValidator` in `convex/server` declares `splitCursor: v.optional(v.union(v.string(), v.null()))` and `pageStatus: v.optional(v.union(..., v.null()))`. A `v.object` return validator refuses fields it does not declare ('Object validators don't allow extra properties, objects with properties that aren't specified will fail validation', docs.convex.dev/functions/validation, read 2026-10-01), so `listOpenOrders` as pinned throws a return-validation error on every call, and Sc L2-2's subscription never gets a value. ledger.issue: Lead 4 holds. `typeEffectHandler` declares `runtime: "convex" | "node"` and the lease differs by it ('35 minutes for the Convex runtime, 15 minutes for Node'), but the Spec registers one action per kind, `export const callProvider = internalAction(...)` and `reconcileAttempt`, both under `internal.effects.*` beside `claimAttempt`, `settleAttempt`, `expireLease` (mutations) and `readForCall` (a query); `claimStep6` schedules `internal.effects.callProvider` or `internal.effects.reconcileAttempt` without reading `runtime`; and `typeEffectRegistry` is 'a static module imported by the actions', which `claimStep3` ('resolve the handler') and `claimStep5` (the policy) must import too. On current Convex this cannot hold a Node handler. 'Files with the `"use node"` directive should not contain any Convex queries or mutations since they cannot be run in the Node.js runtime. Additionally, files without the `"use node"` directive should not import any files with the `"use node"` directive. Files that contain no Convex functions, like a `convex/utils.ts` file, also need the "use node" directive if they use Node.js-specific libraries' (docs.convex.dev/functions/runtimes, read 2026-10-01); 'other Convex functions cannot be defined in files with the `"use node";` directive' (docs.convex.dev/functions/actions, read 2026-10-01). No component function reads `ctx.auth` or environment variables', under the title 'Components have no ctx.auth' and `evidence.status:documented`. context-component's Design: 'a component cannot read the parent's environment or tables, so everything it needs arrives as arguments or as code'. retention-and-restore's Design: 'the parent may read `process.env` while a component may not'. ledger.issue: The corpus treats whether transaction limits add up across nested calls as unknown: F13 `limitNestedCalls` ('does not say whether the per-transaction limits add up across nested calls and components; Probe 4 stands'), batch-shaped-api ('Probe 4 pending ... the bounds here assume they do'), command-pipeline `subTransactionLimits` ('the design passes none until Probe 4 says whether limits add up across the boundary'). The limits page links to the answer: 'These limits apply to each `query` or `mutation` function. To ensure you're within the limits, there are tools to calculate and limit consumption within a transaction', and that section states 'a mutation or query called by another mutation or query share the overall transaction limits' (docs.convex.dev/production/state/limits#transactions and docs.convex.dev/database/writing-data#write-performance-and-limits, read 2026-10-01). So the corpus's worst-case assumption is the documented behavior for nested calls; a component call is a `ctx.runMutation`, though the page does not name components. The same section documents two tools no Spec uses. `ctx.meta.getTransactionMetrics()` returns `{ used, remaining }` for bytes read, bytes written, documents read, documents written, database queries and scheduled functions. `transactionLimits` on a nested call exists to 'reserve space for work after the nested function call, even if the child reads or writes too much', and the docs' example is a wrapper that runs a nested mutation in a try block and records the failure, which is the local reaction wrapper's shape. Three places pay for not using them: the wrapper's `limitBodyBudget` leaves the settle write unprotected, so a body that exhausts the shared budget makes the catch path fail too and the attempt is spent as a rearm, not recorded as a retryable attempt; every batch stops on hand-derived byte arithmetic where it could stop on measured headroom; and first-experiment `captureDocuments` plans to read documents and bytes 'from the backend's execution records where the local backend exposes them' and records `not exposed` otherwise, while the mutation can read its own totals at step 11. The page states no nesting depth; the open-source backend bounds it at 8 (`MAX_REACTOR_CALL_DEPTH`, crates/common/src/knobs.rs, read 2026-10-01), which the deepest chain here, 4, fits.
ledger.fix: In `spec:facts.f13-transactions-have-limits` replace `limitNestedCalls` with the documented statement and its URL, add the depth bound as read from source, and narrow Probe 4 in `spec:facts.probe-plan` to confirming the sharing across a component boundary and the depth. Drop 'until Probe 4 answers' from the bounds that already assume sharing. In `spec:obligations.local-reaction-wrapper` pass `transactionLimits` to the body call, computed from `ctx.meta.getTransactionMetrics()` minus a stated reserve for the settle patch and the next schedule, and say so in `limitBodyBudget`; do the same for the sweeper's `recoverOne` calls. In `spec:application.first-experiment` make `ctx.meta.getTransactionMetrics()` at the pipeline's step 11 the source of `documentsRead`, `documentsWritten`, `bytesRead` and `bytesWritten`, emitted on the diagnostic record. Record under E-22 or E-40 that a batch may stop on measured headroom, with the byte arithmetic kept as the planning bound.

ledger.issue: d02's Decision context states as a Convex fact: 'Convex gives components whose tables the parent cannot read except through the component's own functions, and gives no global sequence, so a global position would have to be a counter document in every write's path'. Current Convex gives one. 'A commit timestamp represents the time (in nanoseconds) when a mutation commits ... with the `db.vars.commitTs` placeholder you can have the value inserted at commit time into documents'; 'You could define an index on a field that captures the commit time, then use that to iterate over new or updated documents without worrying about missing changes due to out-of-order commits'; the comparison table lists 'Reflects commit order: Yes' against `_creationTime` 'No'; 'the timestamp is strictly increasing' (docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/commit-timestamp, read 2026-10-01). `ctx.meta.getSnapshotTs()` gives the matching upper bound: 'no new documents will be written with a `commitTs` at or below this' (docs.convex.dev/api/interfaces/server.QueryMeta, read 2026-10-01). So an order token that costs no counter document and no contention exists, and it does prove that a reader has seen every committed row up to the snapshot. The doc's own rule, 'Timestamps, `_creationTime` and UUID order never prove that a consumer has seen every committed event', is still right for `_creationTime` and `recordedAt` and is not right for a commit timestamp. Nothing fails, and the doc's decision stands until the owner rules. But the reason d02 gives for rejecting a global position is no longer a fact, the ordered consumer of D18 pays 'a write to every command that produces a selected event' for a sequence the engine can now supply, and the history view's cross-stream order problem (r3-architecture-history-fold-order-and-deletion) has a native answer the corpus does not weigh.

ledger.issue: Residue of r2-convex-convex-restore-stream-check-bytes. restore `limitCheckBatch` gives the worst case of one stream-check batch as 'one 600-event fold of at most 17 KiB per event, about 10 MiB, plus the `list` page of at most 2 MiB of stream rows, plus the same rows read again when each `rebuild` re-reads its row before folding, at most 2 MiB, plus the run record, about 14 MiB'. Each `rebuild` call also reads its stream's baseline event: journal `rebuildReads` ranges `by_stream` with `.gte("streamVersion", baselineVersion ?? 1)`, 'the baseline event first when there is one', and `maxEvents` counts only the tail after it (`streamVersion - (baselineVersion ?? 0)`). A baseline payload is bounded by `budgetBytes`, so a batch of `floor(2 MiB / budgetBytes)` streams that each carry a baseline reads up to 2 MiB more: 8 baselines of 256 KiB at the default budget, or 4 of 512 KiB for a derived mapping. The worst case is then about 10 + 2 + 2 + 2 MiB, 16 MiB before the run record, at the read ceiling ('Data read 16 MiB', docs.convex.dev/production/state/limits, read 2026-10-01), where the Spec says 14. A batch that crosses it throws a read-limit error at the same cursor on every run, because a mutation is deterministic. The case needs every stream of the batch migrated at full budget and a tail total at the fold bound, so it is rare, but the stated bound is not below the ceiling as rubric item 29 asks.
ledger.fix: In spec:application.restore include each baseline event and run-record overhead in the cumulative stream-check budget. Lower the stream or tail bound to reserve that headroom, and keep budget refusal resumable at the exact stream position. If metrics are used, await the pinned transaction-metrics API and use metrics.bytesRead.remaining from the resolved result, whose bytesRead metric has { used, remaining } fields. Prove the maximum baseline and tail case on the native backend.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, APPL-08: At HEAD, restore.sdp.md:106 budgets "about 14 MiB" without the baseline events read by journal.sdp.md:96, so the stated 600-event case with three 2 MiB allowances totals about 15.96 MiB before overhead. The issue and counting baselines remain right; the fix's optional metric clause must use the awaited { used, remaining } API rather than accessing bytesRead.remaining on the unresolved promise. The build must show: Native backend stream-check batches must combine full-budget baselines and maximum admitted tails, include run-record overhead and advance or refuse resumably before the shared read ceiling, with no repeated failure at one cursor.

ledger.issue: queries `fnList` caps `numItems` and `maximumRowsRead` at the same number, `limitListPage`, and `fnHistory` does the same with `limitHistoryPage`. In the helper the row cap is tested before the item target: `if (maxRowsToRead !== undefined && indexKeys.length >= maxRowsToRead) hitLimit = true`, then `if (hitLimit) { pageStatus = "SplitRequired"; splitCursor = ... }` (convex-helpers 0.1.124, packages/convex-helpers/server/stream.ts `paginate`, read 2026-10-01). ledger.issue: Every byte bound in the corpus exists to stay under Convex's 16 MiB and 1 MiB ceilings, but the bounds are measured in a different unit and one of them is not checked at run time. journal `limitPayloadBytes`: '`append` measures each validated payload as the byte length of its JSON serialization'. idempotency `fnCanonicalJson`: 'serializes with object keys sorted, `undefined` members omitted, numbers in shortest round-trip form'. Two problems follow from the values `v` validators accept. (1) A payload or an input may hold `v.int64()` or `v.bytes()`; `JSON.stringify` throws on a BigInt and turns an ArrayBuffer into `{}`, so the measure and the fingerprint are undefined for values the declared validators admit ('the same data types supported by function arguments, return types and the database', docs.convex.dev/database/types, read 2026-10-01). (2) Convex ships the measure its limits use: 'Use `getDocumentSize` from "convex/values" to measure the size of documents, including the default `_id` and `_creationTime` fields. Use `getConvexSize` to measure the byte size of arbitrary values'; `getConvexSize` 'matches how Convex calculates document size for bandwidth tracking and size limit enforcement' (docs.convex.dev/database/types#measuring-document-sizes and docs.convex.dev/api/modules/values#getconvexsize, read 2026-10-01), and `convexToJson` gives a JSON form that keeps Int64 and Bytes. Separately, `budgetBytes`, 'the one number every byte-derived bound reads', is never enforced: state-document-mapping `budgetCheck` is 'a native test [that] writes the largest state the product allows', and the adapter's step 9 saves the row without measuring it, while the list page, the streams per call, the backfill batch, the baseline batch and the restore check all assume no row exceeds its budget. A row that grows past its declared budget and stays under 1 MiB is written without error and then breaks those bounds as read-limit errors far from the cause.
ledger.fix: On `spec:context.journal` measure the payload with `getConvexSize` from `convex/values` and state the 16,384-byte bound in that unit; say the same in `spec:constraints.events-stay-small` `measurableBy`. On `spec:context.persistence-adapter` add to step 9 a check that `getDocumentSize` of the row, plus its parts under a derived mapping, is at most `registration.mapping.budgetBytes`, a plain error and a technical failure above it, and name it in `spec:kernel.state-document-mapping` as the run-time enforcer beside `budgetCheck`. On `spec:command.idempotency-and-receipts` define `canonicalJson` over `convexToJson(value)` with keys sorted, so Int64 and Bytes fingerprint deterministically, or state that command inputs admit no `v.int64()` and no `v.bytes()` and have the registration check enforce it. Measure `bounds.maxBytes` and the 16 KiB `details` bound the same way.
ledger.note: S1, 2026-10-01, rulings R8 and F4. Every bound S1 built is measured with `getConvexSize`: the payload in `append` (`spec:context.journal`, `spec:constraints.events-stay-small`), the saved row at the adapter's step 9 (`spec:context.persistence-adapter`, named in `spec:kernel.state-document-mapping`), `bounds.maxBytes` at step 1 and a rejection's `details` in `reject`; `canonicalJson` is `convexToJson` with keys sorted. ledger.issue: Two statements about what a restore does go beyond the pages. The backup page says a backup lacks 'Pending scheduled functions' and that restoring 'wipes your existing data and replaces it with that from the backup' (docs.convex.dev/database/backup-restore, read 2026-10-01). It does not say what happens to functions already pending in the target deployment when a restore runs in place, and F12 itself notes 'The page does not say what restore does to component data or to the scheduler'. If they survive, a pending `callProvider` scheduled before the restore runs after it without passing `claimAttempt`, the only place the dispatch switch is read, so a provider call can go out while `OBLIGATIONS_DISPATCH` is off, against Sc L3-7; a surviving rebuild batch or wrapper is held by the door or the fence. Probe 7 as written 'takes a backup with pending scheduled functions ... restores it, and records what survives', which tests what the backup carries, not what the target keeps. (2) restore's flow: 'The operator restores the snapshot into the target from the dashboard or the CLI import; the restore is destructive and replaces the parent's table data'. The two are not the same operation. `npx convex import --replace` replaces 'existing data in tables mentioned in the ZIP file' and 'Data import only affects tables that are mentioned in the import'; the destructive form is `--replace-all`, 'deleting tables that don't appear in the import file or the schema, and clearing tables that appear in the schema but not in the import file'; the command also takes `--component <path>` (docs.convex.dev/database/import-export/import and docs.convex.dev/cli/reference/import, read 2026-10-01). With `--replace`, a table written after the backup and absent from the ZIP keeps its rows, so 'anything committed after the backup time is outside the restored state' does not hold. Neither page says a ZIP export or a dashboard restore covers component tables; the Spec marks that part as Probe 7's, which is right.

ledger.issue: Rounds 1 and 2 moved the adapter, the list page, the backfill, the baseline batch and the restore's stream check from document counts to bytes. Six batches still state a bound in documents only, and at the corpus's own row ceilings each crosses 'Data read 16 MiB' or 'Data written 16 MiB' per transaction (docs.convex.dev/production/state/limits#transactions, read 2026-10-01), against rubric item 29. (1) `receipts.sweep`: 'at most 1,000 receipts per run for one tenant ... so one run stays far under the 16,000 documents written per transaction' (idempotency `limitSweepBatch`, receipt-table `fnSweep`). receipt-table `limitRowSize` lets a row reach 400 KiB; the receipt of the experiment's own 100-line `PlaceOrder` holds 101 affected refs and 101 stream versions, about 30 KiB, so 1,000 such rows read about 29 MiB. A mutation is deterministic, so a sweep that crosses the ceiling fails at the same rows on every run and expired receipts are never removed. (2) restore `fnReceiptCheckBatch`: '25 receipts per receipt batch, each one component call', where the call is `byOperation`, which 'ranges `by_operation` and collects' every event of the operation; 25 receipts at 400 KiB are 9.8 MiB before any event, and one operation may have appended up to 8 MiB of events (adapter `limitDocumentsWrittenPerCall`), so the batch has no byte bound at all. A failed check batch leaves the restore closed. (3) rebuild `limitPurgeBatch`: '500 rows deleted per purge batch, one index range, under 1 second'; at the 64 KiB `rowBudgetBytes` ceiling 500 rows read 31 MiB, while the backfill beside it is derived from the same budget. (4) sweeper `limitSweepBatch`: '100 candidates per scan and 100 expired leases per scan as the document bound, so one run reads at most about 400 documents', with an inline payload of up to 64 KiB on each row (record-contract `limitInlinePayload`) and each candidate read again inside `recoverOne`, up to about 19 MiB under the shared limits. (5) retention `limitRetentionBatch`: '500 deletions and 500 compactions per run ... under the 16,000 writes per transaction', up to 32 MiB read for the deletions alone. (6) fan-out `limitFanOutPage`: '500 derived obligations per fan-out attempt ... under the 1000 schedules per mutation and the write ceilings', which at a 64 KiB payload writes 31 MiB. The first three are Layer 1 and 2 and sit in the first experiment's path.
ledger.fix: Derive sweep, receipt-check, purge, retention and fan-out bounds from complete measured row and event costs, including rereads, metadata and schedules. Page operation history with a resumable byte and row bound and persist caller progress across pages. At 64 KiB, floor(4 MiB / 64 KiB) is 64, not 62, and payload size alone is not row cost. If transaction metrics select headroom, await the pinned API and read metrics.bytesRead.remaining from the resolved result; each metric has { used, remaining } fields. Preserve provisional numeric defaults until native backend boundary cases prove progress within shared limits.

ledger.issue: The sweeper reads up to 100 dispatch rows per run with `ctx.db.system.get("_scheduled_functions", dispatchId)` inside its mutation and leaves the pending ones alone. A read in a mutation joins its read set, and system tables are no exception: 'You can read data from system tables using the `db.system.get` and `db.system.query` methods, which work the same as the standard `db.get` and `db.query` methods. Queries reading from system tables are reactive and realtime just like queries reading from all other tables' (docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/system-tables, read 2026-10-01). Each scheduled function rewrites its own row when it completes; for a scheduled mutation the completion is written in the mutation's own commit (get-convex/convex-backend crates/application/src/scheduled_jobs/mod.rs, `SchedulerModel::complete` before the commit, read 2026-10-01). So every dispatch that finishes between the sweeper's read and its commit, a window of up to the 500 ms guard, invalidates the sweep, and Convex re-runs it. The condition under which the sweeper reads many pending rows is a draining backlog, Sc L3-3, which is when those rows change fastest, so the sweep keeps losing to the work it is watching, and as a cron job 'following runs of the cron job may be skipped' while one is still retrying (docs.convex.dev/scheduling/cron-jobs, read 2026-10-01). The Spec records the nested-call cost and the time guard and says nothing of this contention. Related to r3-architecture-sweeper-scan-blocked-by-backlog, which is about which rows the scan reaches.

State why a stale answer is safe: a stale `pending` only leaves the candidate for the next tick, a `failed` or `canceled` row never changes again, and `recoverOne` re-reads the obligation and fences on the attempt ID before it rearms. Record the contention as a risk and add it to the sweeper's bound test.

The issue holds; the stale-read fix needs its monotonic-state safety argument and pinned API proof before adoption, and recovery progress needs native backend measurement. The build must show: A native backend draining-backlog comparison must report recovery progress and retries; any stale-read alternative must first have a pinned API check and a safety argument for stale pending and immutable failed/cancelled states, with attempt fencing preventing unsafe rearm.

ledger.issue: During an online rebuild every live command and every backfill batch meet on one document. The pipeline's step 9 calls `generationsToWrite`, which makes 'at most two indexed reads' of `by_read_model_state` and so reads the row of the generation in `building`, `verifying` or `verified`. The same row is the batch's checkpoint: 'The generation row carries the backfill cursor, the verify cursor, the fence and the counts, and a batch writes them in the same mutation as its rows' (generation-registry Contract), and `step5` 'patches the generation row with the new cursor, the counts and `updatedAt`' on every batch, with batches chained by `ctx.scheduler.runAfter(0, ...)`. Convex decides conflicts on the read set: 'At the end of the transaction, the writes all commit if every version in the read set is still the latest version of that record' (docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ, read 2026-10-01), and a write to a document inside a range a mutation read conflicts whatever field changed ('any change to the "tasks" table will conflict with the `writeCount` mutation', docs.convex.dev/error#1, read 2026-10-01). So each batch commit invalidates every command on that read model that is in flight, on any tenant, and the command re-runs. A caller's mutation gets a bounded number of retries, after which 'some of the invocations will eventually throw this error' (same page). With batches committing back to back, a short command re-runs now and then and a long one, the 100-line `PlaceOrder`, overlaps a batch commit on most tries and can exhaust its retries, for the whole length of the rebuild. The corpus says the opposite: 'The common rebuild costs no downtime' (rebuild value), 'The registry is data that changes only during a rebuild, so it is not an application-wide counter in the write path' (generation-registry), and it records the one-time re-run for the gate ('a gate change makes every concurrent command re-run once') but not this repeated one. Probe 6 races a batch against a command on a read-model row, not on the registry row. How often a command loses is unmeasured; that it conflicts on every overlapping batch commit is documented behavior.
ledger.fix: In `spec:application.generation-registry` split the row: keep on `generations` only what a command and a query read, `readModel`, `generation`, `projectionVersion`, `state`, `pauseRequired` and `fence`, which change at start, switch, resume, rollback and abort; move `cursor`, `verifyCursor`, `batchSize`, `batchesDone`, `rowsWritten`, `rowsSkipped`, `misses`, `lastError` and `updatedAt` to a `generationProgress` table keyed by generation ID that only batches and operators read. A batch then checks state and fence on the registry row, which it reads and does not write, and checkpoints on the progress row, which no command reads. Update rebuild's steps 1 and 5, `resumeChain`, the restore's inventory and `finishRestoreRun` to the two rows. Add the registry-row case to Probe 6 in `spec:facts.probe-plan` and to the first experiment's contention run: `PlaceOrder` at the maximum while a backfill runs, counting retries and exhaustions.

The issue and separate progress-row fix remain right; the frequency and throughput consequence need native backend measurement, not convex-test. The build must show: Source review must show disjoint command-selection and batch-checkpoint write sets, and a native backend comparison must run maximum-size and unrelated-stream commands during backfill against a no-rebuild control, reporting retries and exhaustions rather than inferring throughput from convex-test.

Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.

ledger.issue: Several example steps were positive sentences whose bound value negated them: 'is stored {stored: false}', 'returns an identity {anonymousHasIdentity: false}', 'is stored after the parent caught the error and committed {childRowStored: false}'. A reader takes the sentence for the claim. The Probe 2 examples also named 'a client whose parent lets the error pass', a second parent no Given set up. Opus review, minors 4 and 5.
ledger.fix: Reword with counts, and set up every actor in a Given.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01, ruling S6. Steps now bind counts ('holds {rows: 0} rows') or carry no slot ('returns no identity'). Both Probe 2 examples have a Given for the two parents, the one that catches and the one that lets the error pass. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.

ledger.issue: The probe examples wrote the expected answer in as the pass condition with nothing saying it was a hypothesis, so a contrary result would read as a red test to repair: the depth example bound 8 and the first native run showed 9. Probe 3 dropped function-call quota without saying so and its local timings would feed OQ1 unmarked. Probe 5's question, whether the client hook splits a page, sat in a verification bullet that allowed the run to skip it. Probe 1's Thens passed without reaching the guarantee's boundary: twenty trials with no row passed, the HTTP example lost no response, and a random kill might never land before the commit; the examples said 'WebSocket client' for a fact about the React client. The subscription example did not require a parent that reads no table of its own. Opus review, M5 to M8 and minors 5, 6 and 16; the first native run of the probes on 2026-10-01.
ledger.fix: Say in the probe plan what a bound value is and what follows a different result; make each example fail when its boundary is not reached; name the client; give the hook its own example; say what a local backend cannot answer.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01, ruling S7. `spec:facts.probe-plan` carries extension E-16 with six rules: a probe is example Specs that verify its fact; bound values are the expectation written before the first run; a different first result is recorded on the fact and the example is then bound to what the release does and says so; an example fails when its run did not reach its boundary; sizes are recorded and not asserted; what a local backend cannot answer stays open on the fact. Probe 1's three examples name `ConvexClient` or `ConvexHttpClient`, require a trial committed without confirmation, a kill on each side of the commit, and a lost response with one request per call. Probe 3 says quota is not measured and the time is a local backend's. Probe 4's depth binds 9 as observed and calls it a backend default; the shared-limit examples say the seeding is paced under the local backend's write rate and that each half of the write commits alone. Probe 5 gains `probe-5-hook-splits-across-boundary`; the subscription example's parent reads no table of its own. Opus minor 16, drop the depth example, is rejected: the round-3 finding on nested limits asks for the depth and the test is small. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.

ledger.issue: `spec:context.queries` relays a component list's `paginator` page through the parent and relies on the client hook to split a page the helper marks `SplitRequired` (`componentPagination`, `paginationShape`, `parentPassThrough`). On a native backend, release `precompiled-2026-09-28-5c7cb5b`, with `convex-helpers` 0.1.124, the `usePaginatedQuery` hook of `convex-helpers/react` showed 40 of 45 rows after a page of 10 grew to 25 rows under `maximumRowsRead` 20: the five rows between the capped page's `continueCursor` and its end cursor were never loaded, and the hook reported no error. Read in the helper's source by the design agent: a capped page returns `continueCursor` at the last row it read, and the hook ends the second half of the split there. Reading the two halves directly, from the start to the split cursor and from the split cursor to the page's own end cursor, gives all 25 rows. So a list that is capped by `maximumRowsRead` and read with this hook can lose rows without a sign. Found by the design agent's bound test in slice S0, 2026-10-01, run twice; the orchestrator reran it after applying the prototype.
ledger.fix: Slice S2 decides before it builds lists: whether a context list sets `maximumRowsRead` at all, whether the parent or the client closes the range to the page's end cursor, or whether the client uses another hook. The Probe 5 example keeps the observed value so a later helper release that fixes it turns the test red.
ledger.note: S2, 2026-10-02, fold-in after the build. No hook crosses the component boundary: a client pages by the cursor pair and replaces a `SplitRequired` page with two halves to its end cursor (`spec:context.queries`). Shown at the native tier on the fixture composition by `tests/native/context-queries.test.ts`, a page that outgrows its row cap splits into two halves that hold every row, and `tests/native/f15-parent-query-over-component-query-stays-reactive.probe-5-parent-page-outgrows-row-cap.test.ts`; the hook's Probe 5 example keeps its observed value. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.

ledger.issue: F11, 'Components have no `ctx.auth`', is listed by the doc as documented, and the components page says `ctx.auth` is not available within a component. On a native backend, release `precompiled-2026-09-28-5c7cb5b` with `convex` 1.46.0, `ctx.auth.getUserIdentity()` inside a component query returned the caller's identity (the unbound native test `component-auth.test.ts` records it; the run's record is `evidence/native-20261001T162936Z-ba5eddd.json`). `convex-test` 0.0.60 returns null for the same call. Six Specs state as fact that components have no `ctx.auth` or never see it. The design does not depend on which holds: D11 passes the actor explicitly and no component function reads `ctx.auth`. But a reader takes 'cannot read the caller's identity' as an isolation guarantee, and on this backend it is a convention. Opus review of the foundation, M1; ruling O2.
ledger.fix: The owner rules whether F11's wording and status follow the documentation or the backend. Provisional reading, recorded as an open question on F11: the documentation's sentence stands as the fact, the observation is recorded beside it, and the rule that no component function reads `ctx.auth` is a design rule under D11 and not a consequence of the platform.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01. The observation is an open question on `spec:facts.f11-components-have-no-ctx-auth`. No other Spec changed. S1, 2026-10-01, rulings R4 and S12: the kernel, context and command Specs state that no component function reads `ctx.auth` as the design's rule, enforced by ESLint; F11 keeps the documentation's sentence and the observation, and its open question records the provisional reading. The decision Specs D10 and D11 transcribe the doc and are unchanged. Status stays `owner`.

ledger.issue: Extension E-16 said what a different first run means and nothing about a different later run. Seven bound values are what one backend release or one package version does (the depth of 9, the hook's 40 shown and 5 missing, the socket wait, two refusal texts, one log record per call), so the next pin bump would turn them red with nothing saying that red is a finding and not a regression. No example whose expectation held said so. The size rule ('an example asserts a size only where the fact states a bound') forbade the depth example's own Then. Opus review of the fold-in, M1 and M5.
ledger.fix: Say what a red on a new release is; let a reader tell a held expectation from an observed value; rule between the size rule and the depth example.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01. `spec:facts.probe-plan` gains the rule that a later run showing another value is again a finding and the example is rebound, and the size rule now tells a measured size, which is recorded and not asserted, from a limit the backend enforces, which is bound as observed. `spec:platform.native-harness` gains the same rule for the values its four examples bind. Twelve probe examples say their bound values held on the first run; the depth and hook examples already said theirs were observed. The depth example also binds the refusal's text. Read against the Spec text; what is left is s0-e16-silent-on-a-later-different-run-remainder.

ledger.issue: One rule said a fault enters a native run only through something the fixture composition supplies, while other rules and the Design entries give the harness a kill, a closed client and a lost response, and all of Probe 1 injects its fault that way. A slice S1 implementer would read the first rule as forbidding the tools the Spec hands over. Opus review of the fold-in, M2.
ledger.fix: One statement of which faults come from the harness and which only from fixture code.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01. Two rules: a fault inside a function enters only through what the fixture composition supplies; a fault outside the functions, a killed backend, a closed client or a lost response, comes from the harness's controls. Read against the Spec text; what is left is s0-fault-rule-contradicts-the-harness-controls-remainder.

ledger.issue: After the design pass the harness Spec's Design section held about thirty entries under a preamble that called all of them observations: the stubs slice S1 builds on, implementation detail that goes stale at the first code change (system query names, CLI flags, retry counts, thirteen fields copied from the backend's log), and readings of one backend release written as rules. The fixture token was said to yield 'the shape a production token yields' while it carries five claims. Opus review of the fold-in, M3 and minor 10; the owner's direction that a Spec carries the design of its key abstractions.
ledger.fix: Keep the stubs later slices build on, mark one release's readings as readings, drop the entries whose only reader is the harness's own code.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01. Ten entries are gone: the table-read and log mechanisms, the executable resolver and its type, the pin file, the issuer constructor, `startBackend`, the readiness check, the completion record's full type and the CLI call. Three entries are renamed `observedWriteRate`, `observedFunctionLog` and `observedTableRead` and the preamble says they are readings, not rules. `identity` names the five claims the fixture token carries. `adminReads` names the six fields of a completion record a test may rely on. Left for polish: several rules are still said twice or hold two rules in one bullet (Opus minors 1 and 2). Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.

ledger.issue: The component refusal example said Convex 'refuses the call on every route', and for the WebSocket route it showed only that a promise stayed pending for three seconds. The test passed when the mutation was never sent, which the behavior review showed, and when the public route called a function that does not exist, which a native mutation showed. Opus review M4, astra review 6, sol review 6.
ledger.fix: The outcome says what each route showed; the socket step shows that the request left the client and that the backend closed the connection; the public route checks its target.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01. The outcome now reads: refused on the two HTTP routes with its own error, connection closed on the WebSocket route without an answer. The socket step binds the wait and at least one close by the backend, and the verification bullets say what would show a call that ran. The test follows in fold-in 2. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.

ledger.issue: The harness rule said a run 'never signals a process it did not start'. The sweep signals by process id after reading the process table, and between the read and the signal a process id can change hands. The review of the second fold-in showed the interleaving on a model of the code (astra, report U, finding 1), and showed on a real child process that a failed inspection left the process alive, removed its directory and reported success (finding 2).
ledger.fix: The rule says what the harness does before a signal and what it does when it cannot inspect a process; a Design entry says the interval between read and signal is not closed.
ledger.note: S0, 2026-10-01, third main thread. The rule is split in two: cleanup, and inspection before a signal with the failed-inspection case. Design entry `sweepOwnership` states the open interval and why it matters only for a backend that exits during the sweep. The code follows in fold-in 3, list A, item A1. Read against the Spec text; what is left is s0-sweep-rule-promises-more-than-a-process-id-allows-remainder.

ledger.issue: Authorization checks the new input subject, but a conflicting receipt key discloses the stored operation ID for another subject. The unsupported-version answer carries the same metadata.
ledger.fix: Omit stored receipt metadata from conflict and unsupported-version answers unless the actor is authorized for the stored subject. Prove both branches with two actors and two subjects, then check the public answer on the native backend.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, CORE-01. Evidence recorded by that read: convex-test. Counterexample: Bob creates document B with a shared request key; Alice, granted only A, submits A with that key and receives B's stored operation ID on conflict, with the unsupported-version branch exposing the same pointer. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: command/tenancy-and-authority.sdp.md:48 requires authorization before stored outcome disclosure. Fixed on fix/platform-review: the Spec text in 096db7e, the fix in 24ecbce, the proof in e68e0af, merged in 9d63c3f. A conflict and an unsupported-version answer carry a fixed message and no details; the one fact their codes disclose is whether the stored contract version is the declaration's. Proven at the pure test, convex-test and native backend tiers. Read against the Spec text; what is left is pr1-architecture-receipt-conflict-discloses-other-subject-remainder.
ledger.detector: convex-test must cover both branches with two actors and two subjects: B stays forbidden, no B operation ID, result, affected subject or version is disclosed, and state and receipts do not change. Native backend tests must assert the public wire answer while preserving authorized same-input replay and ordinary conflicts.

ledger.issue: The outer boundary checks bare rejection codes but passes tagged errors unchanged, allowing an undeclared code, another command name or oversized details.
ledger.fix: Validate bare and tagged rejections against the running command, its allowed codes and the details bound. Treat invalid tagged rejections like undeclared bare codes and test the helper and a registered command.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, CORE-02. Evidence recorded by that read: pure test. Counterexample: A tagged rejection with code notDeclared and command SomeOtherCommand passes normalization for CreateDocument; a directly constructed tagged error can also bypass the details bound. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: command/outcome-boundary.sdp.md:58 closes the codes, but :76 rethrows errors already carrying kind unchanged. Fixed on fix/platform-review: the Spec text in 096db7e and c233023, the code in 24ecbce, 9d63c3f and efa95da. Every rejection candidate, bare or in the wire shape, passes one validation at the outer boundary, and one that does not fit becomes a plain error. Proven at the compiled, pure test and convex-test tiers, and by native probes of the unit's review. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.
ledger.detector: Pure tests must cover bare and tagged allowed and undeclared codes, wrong command identity, oversized details, malformed tagged data, transient errors and unchanged technical throws. A convex-test registered command calling the helper incorrectly must produce the boundary's technical-failure behavior and preserve rollback.

ledger.issue: Valid caller metadata can make an event larger than the 17 KiB assumed by fold and migration bounds. A 32 KiB correlation ID alone invalidates the 600-event arithmetic.
ledger.fix: Bound caller-set envelope fields at command entry and derive the complete event maximum. Use it in fold, query and migration bounds, with an explicit refusal for metadata past its bound.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, CORE-03. Evidence recorded by that read: convex-test. Counterexample: A valid 32 KiB correlation ID is copied onto every small-payload event; 600 such IDs alone exceed 18.75 MiB, although future folds assume about 17 KiB per complete event. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: context/event-envelope.sdp.md:45 limits only payload bytes and document structure; context/journal.sdp.md:97,108 and context/queries.sdp.md:93 assume about 1 KiB of envelope. The future read-limit claim is arithmetic, not a native failure. Fixed on fix/platform-review: the Spec text in 096db7e and 86da870, the code in 24ecbce and 9d63c3f. Every text field a caller sets is bounded in UTF-8 bytes at step 1, the stream ID at the adapter, and append bounds the envelope at 4,096 bytes, so a stored event is at most 20,541 bytes and the fold bound is 500 events. Proven at the pure test and convex-test tiers and for multibyte text on the native backend. A native run over history of the maximum size waits for the unit that builds rebuild. Read against the Spec text; what is left is pr1-convex-event-envelope-has-no-byte-bound-remainder.
ledger.detector: Pure or convex-test boundary cases must cover exact and one-byte-over limits, multibyte metadata and large actor or delegation fields. Before rebuild bounds are claimed, native backend tests must fold and migrate maximum permitted complete envelopes within shared limits or return the declared refusal, including valid stored history outside a later limit.

ledger.issue: The rebuild helper used a nullish fallback, so an explicit null baseline became the initial state.
ledger.fix: Use an undefined check to distinguish no baseline from an explicit null, and test omitted, null, zero and object starts.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, CORE-04. Evidence recorded by that read: pure test. Counterexample: A decider whose initial state is 42 and whose state admits null rebuilt no tail events from an explicit null start as 42. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: kernel/decider-contract.sdp.md:59 already says start === undefined at this commit; initial-state.sdp.md:44 folds from the baseline state. Commit 2e20b29 fixed it; status is fixed with unreviewed true pending the unit review under response R4. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.
ledger.detector: Pure tests must preserve omitted, null, zero and object starts and show initial is never called for explicit null; commit 2e20b29 already supplies the undefined check, with the fixed item awaiting review.

ledger.issue: The native acceptance example binds every Layer 0 to 2 scenario, but its test runs one sequential path and establishes no concurrency parity.
ledger.fix: Name the path the bound test runs. Add a separate experiment check over required scenarios, compositions, tiers and verifiers that fails when a required case is absent or failing.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, APPL-11. Evidence recorded by that read: source inspection of native test binding. Counterexample: The bound native step says every Layer 0 to 2 scenario but runs a short sequential path; failing a different required scenario does not fail it, and no concurrent commands run. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: application/first-experiment.native-acceptance-production-configuration.sdp.md:25 says every scenario; :32 describes a small end-to-end path. No new native runtime failure is claimed. Fixed on fix/platform-review: c245407 renames the bound steps to the path the test runs, e095da6 adds the acceptance check (npm run acceptance), efa95da and c3f3fd8 harden it. The check derives the required scenarios from the graph and reads one run record; at 645130f it answers 30 passed and 5 missing. Proven at the pure test tier and by a clean run of every tier. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.
ledger.detector: Pure tests must remove and fail a required scenario and make aggregate experiment acceptance fail, with each required scenario mapped to composition, tier, verifier and saved result. The native backend smoke path must retain its actual assertions and fixture-issuer difference; a native contention case is required before claiming concurrency parity.

ledger.issue: Final stream versions do not reveal how many events a command appended, and the diagnostic record has no count of read-model rows written.
ledger.fix: Record explicit bounded event and read-model write counters at their producers, or name backend measurements as the source. Test commands with equal final versions but different amounts of work.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, APPL-12. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec inspection. Counterexample: A stream ending at version 100 can have appended one or several events, and versions reveal neither the prior version nor the zero, one or two generation rows written. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: operations/baseline-operations.sdp.md:84 has versions but no work counters; :94,95 attribute the metrics to that record. confirmed against the Spec text by an independent check on 2026-10-02.
ledger.detector: Pure tests must compare commands appending one and two events to an old stream at version 100 and projections writing zero, one and two generation rows; recorded metrics must equal actual work, with bounded detail truncation preserving the required counters.

ledger.issue: The harness anchor covers only its carrier file. Impact lookup for backend.ts and admin.ts reports unknown coverage and misses the owning Spec.
ledger.fix: Give implementation-bearing harness files distinct anchors to the native harness Spec, or require an explicit review fallback for unknown file coverage.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, FOUND-01. Evidence recorded by that read: graph query and source inspection. Counterexample: Changing harness/backend.ts or harness/admin.ts alone gives an empty impact set and unknown coverage, while including the anchor carrier harness/native.ts finds the native-harness Spec. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: Graph recipe 4 reports coverageUnknownFiles for harness/backend.ts and harness/admin.ts. This is a graph gap, not a runtime failure. Fixed on fix/platform-review in c245407: every TypeScript file under harness/ carries its own code anchor, and a pure test fails when one loses it. harness/backend-release.json cannot carry an anchor; SESSIONS.md says a file with unknown coverage is reviewed against the Spec that owns its directory. Confirmed in the Spec text by a lens read.
ledger.detector: Graph recipe 4 must reach spec:platform.native-harness for each implementation-bearing harness file, or the review procedure must require its owning-contract review for unknown coverage. Compiled anchor declarations must remain valid; a graph binding proves location, not a passed runtime test.

ledger.issue: The foundation vocabulary calls a command a request to one context and gives a context one decider. CONTEXT.md instead separates command from stream command and assigns a decider to a stream type. The Spec also prohibits receipt and generation names already used in code.
ledger.fix: Obtain the queued owner ruling on which vocabulary leads, then align the command, stream command, decider, receipt and generation entries and the permitted provisional language.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, FOUND-02. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec and source inspection. Counterexample: A builder following Pack modelRefs gets a command for one context and a context-wide decider, while CONTEXT.md gives a parent command, a stream command and a decider per stream type; the Spec also forbids receipt and generation names already in code. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: No ledger match. platform/vocabulary.sdp.md:37,38 conflicts with CONTEXT.md; :21,25,26 prohibit names already used. STATE.md:183 carries the authority question.
ledger.detector: Source review after the owner's authority ruling must find one meaning for command, stream command, decider, receipt and generation and one permitted provisional naming policy. Compiled declarations using those terms must remain valid; compilation alone cannot prove vocabulary agreement.

ledger.issue: Foundation Specs say nothing has run and the nested-call amount is unmeasured, although retained evidence records probes 1 to 5 and local latency.
ledger.fix: Remove stale work-status sentences or point to dated evidence and STATE.md. Distinguish the measured local latency from the open hosted quota and cost questions.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, FOUND-03. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec inspection and retained native backend records. Counterexample: Foundation Specs say nothing has run and all nested-call cost is unmeasured although their own fact ledger records probes 1 to 5 and F4 records local latency. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: No ledger match. transactional-domain-platform.sdp.md:38 and fact-ledger.sdp.md:22,32 say nothing has run; fact-ledger.sdp.md:15 records the probes. d02-context-owns-state-and-journal.sdp.md:26,30 overstate what remains unmeasured.
ledger.detector: Source review must find no claim that no implementation ran or all Probe 3 work remains pending, with dates, dependency versions and evidence references kept beside facts. Retained native backend records must substantiate local observations while hosted quota and cost stay explicitly unmeasured.

ledger.issue: A restored pending external obligation can repeat an effect that ran after the backup because it has no reconciliation flag. A backup before claim also loses the original provider-key issue time.
ledger.fix: Treat restored external obligations without proof of non-execution as uncertain before dispatch. Preserve or conservatively reconstruct the provider-key validity window.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, DUR-01. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec walkthrough; no runtime result. Counterexample: A backup holds a pending external obligation, the provider succeeds after it, and restore rearms the unflagged old row as a call; a backup before first claim also loses the true provider-key issue time. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: Pending backup, provider success, then restore schedules a call without reconciliation; retention-and-restore.sdp.md:44 promises the check but :67 only tests the old flag, and claim-call-settle.sdp.md:86 stamps a missing issue time. The review rated this blocker; the independent check rated it major because design/specs/obligations/retention-and-restore.sdp.md:44 states the right rule and only the steps fall short of it. confirmed against the Spec text by an independent check on 2026-10-02.
ledger.detector: Native backend and end-to-end provider-stub cases must cover backups before claim, during running and after settlement under every applicable repetition policy, including restore after key expiry. Effect counts and evidence must show one effect or the declared uncertain operator exit, without treating an old pending status or new issue timestamp as proof of safety.

ledger.issue: Joining tenant and effect key with a colon gives the same provider key for distinct pairs containing colons.
ledger.fix: Use a stable injective tuple encoding or a hash of a canonical versioned tuple. Rule on provider-account and deployment scope and test separator-bearing inputs.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, DUR-02. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec walkthrough; no runtime result. Counterexample: Tenant a:b with effect key c and tenant a with effect key b:c both derive a:b:c, although they are distinct valid database identities in one provider account. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: claim-call-settle.sdp.md:64 maps both (a:b, c) and (a, b:c) to a:b:c; record-contract.sdp.md:61 admits strings without separator restrictions. confirmed against the Spec text by an independent check on 2026-10-02.
ledger.detector: Pure tests must distinguish separator-bearing, Unicode, empty-if-admitted and boundary-length tuples across tenants, with stable derivation through retry and restore. A provider-stub test must observe two independent effects for the colliding old tuples; provider-account and deployment scope must be ruled before changing E-58.

ledger.issue: A negative reconciliation says a new call is safe, but reconcileFirst selects reconciliation again. Expired provider keys force reconciliation even when the handler has none.
ledger.fix: Pin mode transitions by current mode, report and policy. Admit a call after proved absence and give expired keys without a safe reconciliation path an explicit needs-attention exit.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, DUR-03. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec walkthrough; no runtime result. Counterexample: Under reconcileFirst, a negative reconcile report retryable schedules reconciliation again until exhaustion; with an expired reuseProviderKey, the next claim forces a scheduled safe call back into reconciliation even when the handler has no reconcile method. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: claim-call-settle.sdp.md:60 permits a call after retryable reconciliation, but :95 selects reconcile again; :74 makes reconcile optional outside reconcileFirst and :86 forces it on expiry. confirmed against the Spec text by an independent check on 2026-10-02.
ledger.detector: A pure transition table must distinguish current mode, report meaning and policy, including confirmed absence versus unavailable reconciliation. Native backend tests must show exactly one call after negative reconciliation under both policies, no blind call after unavailable reconciliation, and an explicit safe exit for expired reuse with and without a reconcile handler.

ledger.issue: Late evidence on a terminal obligation sets reconcileRequested, but operator reconciliation is refused and restore cannot complete while that flag remains.
ledger.fix: Record a resolution of terminal late evidence without changing terminal status. Pin how compensation references that resolution and prevent duplicate compensation.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, DUR-04. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec walkthrough; no runtime result. Counterexample: Cancel an obligation, then receive late provider confirmation: the terminal row keeps reconcileRequested, the operator cannot reconcile it, and restore waits forever for the flag to clear. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: lifecycle-transitions.sdp.md:47 sets the flag without changing terminal status; operator-operations.sdp.md:46 refuses terminal operations; retention-and-restore.sdp.md:70 requires no flag. confirmed against the Spec text by an independent check on 2026-10-02.
ledger.detector: Native backend tests must cancel, receive late confirmation and record a resolution while preserving cancelled status, then complete the restore reconciliation pass. The same evidence must not cause duplicate compensation, and any compensating operation must reference its recorded resolution.

ledger.issue: The local wrapper checks the deadline only before another retry. Neither first execution nor external claim checks it, so queued work can start after expiry.
ledger.fix: Rule on what deadline means and check it at the required execution or admission boundary, including the external action. State whether an operator retry changes the deadline or budget.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, DUR-05. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec walkthrough; no runtime result. Counterexample: A first dispatch waits past its deadline or a write pause spans it; the wrapper admits the body and an external claim schedules a provider action because only later retry admission checks deadline. Spec evidence at 2e20b29: local-reaction-wrapper.sdp.md:61,64 admits the first body and :68 checks only retry time; claim-call-settle.sdp.md:82-88 has no deadline precondition. confirmed against the Spec text by an independent check on 2026-10-02.
ledger.detector: Native backend cases must cover a delayed first dispatch, a pause spanning the deadline and an operator retry of exhausted work. Each must assert the ruled outcome, budget and deadline treatment, with zero prohibited body or provider executions, including delay between external claim and action admission.

ledger.issue: The retention rule promises every repetition horizon, but its bound uses only 30 days and current provider-key validity. Longer upstream contracts and removed or shortened policies lose protection.
ledger.fix: Record accepted repetition horizons or retain a compact identity for their duration. Define how policy changes apply to old work.
ledger.note: the platform review of 2026-10-02, DUR-06. Evidence recorded by that read: Spec walkthrough; no runtime result. Counterexample: A 90-day upstream redelivery contract with a one-day provider key outlives 30-day deletion; removing a handler or shortening current policy can delete protection for work accepted under longer terms.
